name: Aged cheddar cheese
note: Cured cheese is one of the few foods excluded by every published low-histamine diet, and here the measured content supports the exclusion. Ripening time matters more than variety.

ratings.note: Mean histamine in fermented foods surveyed ran 22–74 mg/kg, but the top 5% of cheese samples exceeded 203 mg/kg. The variability is the point: it depends on the hygiene of the raw milk and the histamine-forming capacity of the bacteria used, so two cheeses of the same type can differ greatly.
Tyramine reached 1500 mg/kg in cheese — higher than the histamine levels — and is produced by many of the lactic acid bacteria used in fermentation.

name: Almonds
note: A good illustration of why the unit matters. Both sources below call almonds high in oxalate, but they rank almonds against spinach differently — because one measures per 100 g and the other per serving, and a serving of nuts is far smaller than a serving of greens. Neither is wrong; a reader comparing two food lists without noticing the denominator would think they contradict each other.

ratings.note: 407 mg per 100 g, listed in the same table as spinach at 658 mg.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving — explicitly below the very-high band that holds spinach and rhubarb.
1090 mg per 100 g. The highest figure in the review’s table — above spinach.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Grouped with quinoa as a pseudocereal.
Not detected in seven samples.
3.5 mg total oxalate per 100 g in a single raw Granny Smith sample — one cultivar, one sample.

name: Asparagus
note: The figure is for boiled asparagus specifically. Boiling reduces soluble oxalate, so a raw or roasted preparation is not covered by this number.

ratings.note: 2.6 mg total oxalate per 100 g across three boiled samples.

name: Avocado
note: The two histamine sources differ, and neither is wrong: they measured different produce. Geography, cultivar, storage and assay all move this result.

ratings.note: Five Spanish-market samples were not detected, while one cited report measured 23 mg/kg. Avocado is named as one of only four plant foods with reported histamine.
Not detected in five Brazilian samples.
1.3 mg total oxalate per 100 g fresh weight, two raw samples.

name: Banana
note: Commonly excluded from low-histamine diets for a reason that is not histamine. Worth knowing before eliminating it.

ratings.note: Bananas fall in the 68% of foods excluded by low-histamine diets in which no significant histamine was detected. They do carry putrescine, which has been proposed — on limited evidence, chiefly one 1985 animal study — to compete with histamine for the DAO enzyme. The exclusion may be reasonable; it is not about the banana's histamine content.
Ripeness changes the result; check the app rather than assuming.
Histamine was not detected, but putrescine measured 15–50 mg/kg and banana sits in the paper’s high-other-amines group.
Not detected across twelve samples.
6.8 mg total oxalate per 100 g raw.

name: Beans
note: The two reviews disagree, and the reason is not settled. A later review compiling total oxalate across bean type, form and boiling reports values from 13.9 to 547.9 mg per 100 g. A spread that wide means the two reviews may simply have measured different beans. The differing denominators — per 100 g against per serving — are one candidate explanation, not the answer.

ratings.note: 25 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving.

name: Beer
note: A fermented drink with low measured histamine. That is a statement about content only — see the wine entry for the separate question of what alcohol does to histamine metabolism.

ratings.note: Multiple styles were not detected or below 1.5 mg/L.
61 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving.

name: Brewed coffee
note: The beverage, not the bean: defective green beans gave different results in the same review, so this entry does not cover “coffee” generally.

ratings.note: Regular, decaffeinated and organic coffee beverages were all not detected.

5.6 mg per 100 g. Low per 100 g, but the companion review records a case of oxalate nephropathy attributed to black iced tea in a patient with existing kidney disease — volume can outrun concentration.

name: Canned sardines
note: The exception to an otherwise reassuring picture for fish. Most fishery products carry little histamine — EFSA found it in only 27% of 6,329 European samples, generally at low levels — but where freshness failed before processing, the result is locked in.

ratings.note: 657 mg/kg was measured in canned sardines — the single highest fish figure reported. Sardines are a scombroid species, whose high free histidine content is the substrate spoilage bacteria convert into histamine. Biogenic amines are thermostable, so canning does not reduce what has already formed.
Across Brazilian canned preparations, mostly low but reaching the moderate band in some.

name: Canned tuna
note: Not merged with fresh or frozen tuna. Tuna is a scombroid species, so what happened before canning determines the result — and canning cannot undo it.

ratings.note: Across products and studies, from not detected to above 80 mg/kg. Form, packing medium and study all move it.

name: Chicken breast
note: As with fish, freshness rather than species is what moves this. Histamine forms through bacterial action after death, and no cooking step removes what has already formed.

ratings.note: Values across the fresh-breast series stayed below 10 mg/kg; several other chicken products were not detected or low.

name: Chickpeas
note: The clearest illustration on this site that “low histamine” and “low in all amines” are not the same statement.

ratings.note: Not detected.

Grouped explicitly with foods high in other amines: spermidine 15–85 and spermine 4–32 mg/kg fresh weight. Whether that matters clinically rests on the DAO-competition hypothesis, which is not established.
14.3 mg total oxalate per 100 g for dry seeds, two samples.

name: Cocoa powder
note: Appears both in the oxalate tables and among the foods implicated in reported cases of oxalate nephropathy.

ratings.note: 111 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Also named in this review’s summary of biopsy-proven oxalate nephropathy case reports.

name: Cornmeal
note: Another per-100 g versus per-serving disagreement. Worth noticing that the conflict here is not about the food at all — both reviews would agree on the number.

ratings.note: 25.6 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Listed by name in the high band.
Not detected across ten samples.
Mean histamine across fermented foods ran 22–74 mg/kg, with the top 5% of dry-fermented sausage samples above 130 mg/kg. Excluded by every low-histamine diet reviewed.
Reached 750 mg/kg — produced by the same lactic acid bacteria that drive the fermentation.
Across product types and studies, from not detected to well above 50 mg/kg.
One of only three plant foods in which histamine was actually detected, with tomato and spinach. Accumulation has been linked to bacterial activity during storage, so freshness affects the answer.
Whole, peel, pulp and core measurements span the site’s bands, so no single label represents the food.
Roughly 12.8 to 55 mg total oxalate per 100 g across raw and boiled datasets, crossing the site’s bands.
Most fresh fish showed no histamine or very little, with 95% of samples below 20 mg/kg — but 111 mg/kg was measured in one fresh salmon sample. The variable that moves this is handling, not species.
100 mg per 100 g. Figure is for raw hazelnuts.

name: Ketchup
note: Kept separate from fresh tomato. Processing and storage change the result, and the range here is wide enough that a single figure would misrepresent it.

ratings.note: Reported from not detected to 22 mg/kg, with putrescine from not detected to 165 mg/kg.

name: Kiwi
note: Kiwi illustrates why measured content and a reported trigger must remain separate: its measured histamine is low, while one review records an unconfirmed endogenous-release hypothesis.

potentialTriggers.note: The review names kiwi among foods reported to trigger endogenous histamine release, while stating that the responsible mechanism has not been elucidated.

ratings.note: Ranged from not detected to 2 mg/kg.
Placed in the low-all-amines group.
8 mg per 100 g. Figure is for boiled lentils.
Histamine was not detected, while spermidine measured 15–107 mg/kg.

name: Miso
note: High on two independent axes, which is unusual — most entries here are a concern on one.

ratings.note: Soy-fermented products carried the highest histamine of any category surveyed: 5% of samples exceeded 486 mg/kg, against 203 mg/kg for cheese.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Miso soup is named in the high oxalate band.

name: Mushrooms
note: Another separation between preformed histamine and the other amines, this time consistent across several mushroom types.

ratings.note: Not detected in the reviewed mushroom data.
Putrescine from not detected to 156 and spermidine 9 to 155 mg/kg; placed in the high-other-amines group.
Not detected across Pleurotus, Agaricus, shiitake, portobello, cooked and canned samples, though the individual groups were small.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving.

name: Orange
note: The clearest published example of a food list and a laboratory disagreeing: 60% of reviewed low-histamine diets exclude citrus, and citrus contains no detectable histamine.

ratings.note: No histamine detected in citrus, yet 60% of the ten reviewed low-histamine diets exclude it. What citrus does carry is putrescine, at a mean of 79 mg/kg and up to 173 mg/kg in mandarins — among the highest of any food surveyed.
Citrus putrescine measured 7–200 mg/kg.
Fourteen samples, mean 0.1 mg/kg.
1.8 mg total oxalate per 100 g raw.

name: Papaya
note: The 2018 amine review did not report a histamine figure for papaya, so no histamine rating is recorded against it. A source that did not measure something is not a source saying the value is low.

ratings.note: Placed in the low-all-amines group.
Not detected in the Brazilian samples.
Below the 20 mg per 100 g boundary this site uses for low.
94.5 mg per 100 g. Peanut is also the implicated food in one of the biopsy-proven oxalate nephropathy case reports the companion review summarises.
In the paper’s low-all-amines group — unlike the generic “nuts” grouping it is often folded into.
Low across every measured amine.

name: Pear
note: Rated on one axis only, because one axis is all that was measured. An empty cell here means nothing has been recorded — not that the value is low.

ratings.note: Grouped with foods high in other amines. Histamine was not reported for pear in this review, so no histamine rating is recorded against it.
50 mg per 100 g. Figure is for raw peas, right at the 50 mg high-band threshold.
No significant histamine, but among the foods carrying putrescine at 25–150 mg/kg that published low-histamine diets nonetheless do not exclude.

name: Pineapple
note: Fresh fruit only. A cited study found detectable histamine in processed pineapple juice, so the juice is a different object and is not covered by this entry.

ratings.note: Not detected in the reviewed data.
Placed in the low-all-amines group.
Not detected across the Brazilian samples.
49 mg per 100 g. Just under the 50 mg threshold the companion review uses for its high band — a reminder that the boundary is a convention, not a cliff.
50 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Banded specifically as potatoes with skin, which is where most of the oxalate sits.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Banded as a pseudocereal alongside amaranth.
19.2 mg per 100 g.
433 mg per 100 g.
Topmost band, above 200 mg per serving. Rhubarb also appears in this review's summary of biopsy-proven oxalate nephropathy case reports.
112 mg per 100 g.
Topmost band, above 200 mg per serving. Bran is dense, so a serving carries far more than its per-100 g figure suggests relative to a leafy green.
Named among the fermented products that can accumulate high histamine. Fermented foods were the only category excluded unanimously across all ten diets reviewed.
Fermented vegetables reached tyramine levels up to 1700 mg/kg, the highest of any category measured.
7.1 mg total oxalate per 100 g in the reported raw product.

name: Soy sauce
note: Kept separate from soybeans deliberately. The same starting material, fermented, produces a completely different measurement.

ratings.note: Forty-two samples, mean 123 mg/L, range from not detected to 307. The product-to-product spread is the finding.
77 mg per 100 g.
No significant histamine detected, though soybeans carry relevant amounts of putrescine. Note that fermented soy products are an entirely different matter — see miso.
High putrescine and polyamines, including spermidine up to 389 mg/kg.

name: Spinach
note: Two axes worth separating. Spinach is unambiguously high in oxalate. Its histamine content is a different matter: it is present, and it rises the longer the leaves are stored.

potentialTriggers.note: The comparative review includes spinach among foods described as having possible histamine-releasing capacity, then states that no supporting human clinical studies were found and that the few laboratory or animal studies were inconclusive.

ratings.note: 658 mg per 100 g — the highest single value in the review's table of higher-oxalate foods.
Placed in the topmost band, foods above 200 mg of oxalate per serving.

Histamine is detectable in spinach and increases substantially over refrigerated storage — one cited study measured a significant rise across 15 days. Spinach's relatively high pH permits growth of the bacteria that decarboxylate histidine into histamine, so freshness matters more here than the plant itself does.

name: Star fruit
note: Star fruit also appears in published case reports of oxalate nephropathy. A measured composition figure is a stronger basis for listing it than a case report alone, which is why it is recorded here on the measurement.

ratings.note: 160 and 295.4 mg total oxalate per 100 g across the reported datasets.

name: Strawberry
note: Three independent sources agree the measured content is low on every axis they cover. A separate review signal records the unconfirmed claim that strawberry may trigger endogenous histamine release.

potentialTriggers.note: The review lists strawberry among foods suggested to release endogenous histamine, while emphasizing that there are no supporting human clinical studies and only a few inconclusive laboratory or animal studies.

ratings.note: Not detected. Grouped among foods with low levels of all measured amines.
Putrescine 2–6, cadaverine not detected to 4, spermidine 5–10 mg/kg fresh weight; the remaining measured amines low or not detected.
Not detected in seven samples.
2.9 mg total oxalate per 100 g fresh weight, eight raw samples.

name: Sweet potato
note: Low on one axis and high on another, which is the whole reason these axes are kept apart. The oxalate figure comes from a kidney-stone literature and says nothing about mast cells.

ratings.note: Mean 0.60 mg/kg across three samples.
495.6 mg total oxalate per 100 g fresh weight, two raw samples.

name: Swiss chard
note: Rated high rather than variable: the magnitude moves a great deal between datasets, but every reported total stays above the high boundary.

ratings.note: 874 mg total oxalate per 100 g raw in one dataset and 1458.1 in another, with substantially different leaf/stem and raw/boiled results.
274 mg per 100 g.

potentialTriggers.note: The review includes tomato among foods described as having possible histamine-releasing capacity, while stating that a direct human clinical effect has not been established.

ratings.note: One of the few plant foods in which histamine was actually detected, alongside eggplant and spinach. Levels may be partly physiological, but accumulation has been linked to bacterial activity during storage — so, as with spinach, freshness affects the answer.
Not detected to 9.5 mg/kg across the Brazilian datasets.

name: Watermelon
note: Low on both axes measured, though each dataset behind those figures is small.

ratings.note: 0.7 mg/kg.
0.3 mg total oxalate per 100 g.

name: Whole-grain flour
note: The widest gap between the two reviews. One measured a specific flour; the other banded a whole category. A category band cannot be finer than its coarsest member, which is how a food measured at 11.6 mg per 100 g ends up inside a band defined as above 50 mg per serving.

ratings.note: 11.6 mg per 100 g.
Banded as high, above 50 mg per serving. Covered by the high band as “wholegrain cereals”, a category rather than a specific flour.

name: Wine
note: One of the clearest cases where a food is excluded for what it does to histamine metabolism rather than for the histamine it contains.

ratings.note: Histamine and other biogenic amines in fermented beverages were much lower than in other fermented foods — yet wine is excluded by every low-histamine diet reviewed. The reason offered is not its histamine content: alcohol and its metabolite acetaldehyde compete with histamine for aldehyde dehydrogenase, so drinking alongside histamine-containing food can raise the effective dose from that food.
Low by measured content across the listed wines. The alcohol-metabolism question on this entry is separate and unaffected.

name: Zucchini
note: The reverse of the banana case, and the more revealing one. If putrescine is the reason citrus is excluded, the published diets are not applying that reason consistently.

ratings.note: No significant histamine. Zucchini does carry putrescine, at up to 25–150 mg/kg — the same compound cited to justify excluding bananas and citrus — and yet no reviewed low-histamine diet excludes it. The review names this inconsistency directly.
